analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing sexual harassment claims into private arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, with 18 Senate cosponsors including leading Republicans, was referred to committee and never received a vote, dying when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Most American workers sign employment contracts that require any dispute to be settled in private arbitration rather than in court. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable for sexual harassment and other sex discrimination claims, letting workers take those cases to a public courtroom with a judge and jury. It was introduced with support from senators of both parties and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who experience sexual harassment or sex discrimination on the job — the majority of whom currently sign away their right to sue as a condition of employment. They would be able to file in court, have their case heard publicly, appeal an unfavorable ruling, and join class actions with coworkers. Law enforcement of workplace rights would also shift from private, confidential proceedings into the public record.

how_it_helps.text: A predispute arbitration agreement could no longer be enforced if it requires arbitration of a sex discrimination dispute, so a worker could refuse arbitration and sue in court under Title VII.

A court, rather than an arbitrator, would decide whether the arbitration agreement applies, removing the conflict of interest in which the arbitrator hired by the employer decides their own authority.

The bill applies to conduct that would form the basis of a Title VII sex claim even if no statutory violation is formally alleged, covering the full range of harassment and sex discrimination disputes.

analysis.who_pays: Employers lose the ability to confine harassment claims to private, confidential arbitration, where cases are decided by arbitrators they pay, damages are harder to appeal, and public exposure and class actions are largely eliminated. The arbitration industry loses a significant stream of employment disputes. Larger companies with company-wide arbitration policies bear the adjustment most.

drawbacks.text: Defenders of arbitration argue it can be faster and less expensive for workers than litigation, and that the privacy of arbitration protects complainants from public embarrassment and retaliation — a real trade-off, since a public courtroom also means a public proceeding.
The bill leaves arbitration provisions in collective bargaining agreements untouched, so workers covered by union contracts remain in the union's arbitration process.
The bill covers only sex discrimination disputes, leaving forced arbitration intact for claims of race, age, disability, and wage theft.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is substantial: restoring access to a judge, a jury, public proceedings, and appeal in the most serious workplace discrimination cases. The cost falls mainly on employers, in higher exposure and litigation expense, and on the arbitration industry, in lost business. The bill's main design limitation is its narrow scope — it does nothing for workers facing other kinds of discrimination — and it preserves union-negotiated arbitration. Even an honest supporter would say it was a first step rather than a full fix of mandatory arbitration.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so the bill died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced December 6, 2017, the bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote appear in the action history for the remainder of the 115th Congress.

The bill carried the names of senators from both parties, including Republicans Lindsey Graham and Lisa Murkowski among the original cosponsors, and finished with 18 cosponsors — 15 Democrats and 3 Republicans.
Because Congress adjourned on January 3, 2019, the bill expired without a vote and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that require workers to sign arbitration clauses — and the arbitration industry that serves them — are better off, because nothing changed: sexual harassment claims continue to be resolved in private arbitration, out of public courtrooms, exactly as before.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines — 3 of the 18 cosponsors were Republicans, including Lindsey Graham and Lisa Murkowski — but the bill never reached a vote, so how either chamber would have split is unknown.

industries.note: These companies would lose the power to keep harassment claims in private, employer-paid arbitration and out of the courts, where public exposure, juries, and appeals raise their costs. Ordinary workers are the ones who regain a day in court, so the industry's interest runs against theirs.

Employment disputes are a major revenue source for arbitration firms; the bill removes a large category of cases from their docket. Their revenue depends on proceedings workers cannot take to a judge or jury.
